Cross-linguistic cognates include fr massif ('solid, massive'), es macizo ('solid, sturdy'), en massive / massif ('large and solid / mountain block'); related Italian derivatives include massa ('mass, bulk'), ammassare ('to pile up, amass'). In carpentry and hardware, legno massiccio and ottone massiccio mean solid wood and solid brass (never veneered or plated).
massiccio.notes: In carpentry and hardware, legno massiccio and ottone massiccio mean solid wood and solid brass (never veneered or plated).

matita.etymology: Apheretic alteration (with assimilation of em- to am- and loss of initial a-) of amatita ('red chalk, hematite crayon'), from Classical Latin haematītēs ('bloodstone, red iron ore used for drawing Crayons'), borrowed from Ancient Greek αἱματίτης [λίθος] (haimatítēs, 'blood-like red stone', from αἷμα, haîma, 'blood').

mattina.etymology: Substantivized feminine of Latin mātūtīna (hōra), '(hour) of Matuta', the Roman goddess of the dawn.

morphemes.meaning: of Matuta, goddess of dawn (< Mātūt-)

rootFamily.gloss: morning (slightly more literary; il buon mattino)

mattina.notes: Stamattina ('this morning') fuses questa + mattina, parallel to stasera ('tonight') and stanotte ('last night / tonight').

mattinata.etymology: Derived within Italian from mattina ('morning', < Vulgar Latin *(hōra) mātūtīna) + the duration suffix -ata, designating the whole span or course of a morning.

mattino.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *(tempus) mātūtīnum ('morning time'), substantivized neuter of Classical Latin mātūtīnus ('of the early morning', sacred to Mātūta, the archaic Italic goddess of dawn), with syncope of the pretonic vowel.

history.meaning: early morning time (from Dawn goddess Mātūta)

mattone.etymology: Augmentative of Dialectal/Old Italian matto / maltha ('lump of baked clay, mortar, mudbrick', connected either to Classical Latin maltha < Greek μάλθα, 'pitch-and-lime mortar', or to pre-Roman substrate *matta, 'compact lump').

me.etymology: Continues Classical Latin mē ('me', accusative and ablative singular of ĕgō, 'I'), preserved with closed e as the stressed first-person singular oblique pronoun (dopo di me, con me).

meglio.etymology: Continues Classical Latin mĕlĭus ('better', neuter comparative of bŏnus and comparative adverb of bĕnĕ), with regular Tuscan palatalization of -li- before a vowel to -gli- (/ʎʎ/).

mela.etymology: Continues Late Latin mēla, neuter plural of Classical Latin mālum (Doric Greek μᾶλον, Attic μῆλον, mêlon, 'apple, tree fruit'), reanalyzed in Vulgar Latin as a feminine singular noun (while masculine melo designates the apple tree).

melodia.etymology: Continues Late Latin melōdĭa, from Greek μελῳδία (melōidía, 'singing, choral song'), compound of μέλος (mélos, 'musical phrase') + ᾠδή (ōidḗ, 'song').
melodia.notes: Stress falls on the i (/meloˈdi.a/), following the Greek accent just like armonia and sinfonia.

meno.etymology: Continues Classical Latin mĭnus ('less', neuter comparative of parvus and comparative adverb of parum), with regular lowering of short Latin ĭ to closed e.

menta.etymology: Continues Classical Latin mĕnta / mĭntha ('mint'), borrowed from Ancient Greek μίνθη (mínthē, 'mint', a Mediterranean substrate plant name).

mentalità.etymology: Late 19th-century borrowing modeled on French mentalité (itself after English mentality), built on Late Latin mentālis ('of the mind', from Classical Latin mēns, mentis, 'mind, intellect') + the abstract suffix -ità (< -itātem).
mentalità.notes: Like all Italian nouns ending in -tà (apocopated from Old Italian -tade < Latin -tātem), mentalità is feminine and invariable in the plural.

mentre.etymology: Continues Old Italian domentre, univerbated in Vulgar Latin from Classical Latin dŭm ĭntĕrĭm ('while in the meantime'), with apheresis of the initial syllable.

menu.etymology: Borrowed in the 19th century from French menu ('detailed list of dishes served at a meal'), substantivized from the adjective menu ('small, finely detailed', < Classical Latin mĭnūtus, 'small, minute').

history.meaning: detailed list of dishes, bill of fare

meraviglioso.etymology: Derived from meraviglia ('wonder, marvel', < Late/Vulgar Latin mīrābĭlia, neuter plural of Classical mīrābĭlis, 'wonderful, astonishing', from mīrārī, 'to wonder at') + the suffix -oso (reinforced by Old French merveillos).

mercato.etymology: Continues Classical Latin mercātus, mercātum ('trade, traffic, marketplace, fair'), derived from mercārī ('to trade, buy and sell', from merx, mercis, 'merchandise, wares').

mercoledì.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *Mercŏrī diēs (for Classical Latin Mercŭriī diēs, 'day of Mercury'), preserving the ancient planetary week with dissimilation of the first r to l.

meritare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin mĕrĭtāre ('to earn, deserve, gain'), frequentative of mĕrēre / mĕrērī ('to earn, deserve, merit').

mescolare.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *misculāre, frequentative/diminutive derivative of Classical Latin miscēre ('to mix, mingle').
mescolare.notes: Everyday verb for stirring a pot or shuffling a deck of playing cards (mescolare le carte).

mese.etymology: Continues Classical Latin mēnsis, mēnsem ('month'), with regular Vulgar Latin assimilation of the -ns- cluster to -s-.

messaggio.etymology: Borrowed via Old Provençal messatge / Old French message from Vulgar Latin *missātĭcum ('that which is sent'), from Latin mĭttĕre ('to send').
messaggio.notes: The suffix -aggio (viaggio, coraggio, formaggio, messaggio) regularly marks medieval loans from Gallo-Romance -age/-atge.

metallico.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin mĕtallĭcus ('pertaining to metal or mining'), borrowed from Ancient Greek μεταλλικός (metallikós, from μέταλλον, métallon, 'mine, quarry, metal').

metallo.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin mĕtallum ('metal, mineral, mine'), borrowed from Ancient Greek μέταλλον (métallon, 'mine, quarry, mineral, metal').

metro.etymology: Borrowed via French mètre ('meter', defined during the French Revolution in 1791 as the base unit of length), from Ancient Greek μέτρον (métron, 'measure, rule, standard') via Latin mĕtrum.

history.meaning: meter; tape measure; subway (clipped from metropolitana)

mettere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin mĭttĕre ('to send, let go, throw, cast'), which in Vulgar Latin and Romance shifted semantically to 'to put, place, set' (displacing pōnĕre in everyday use), with regular lowering of short ĭ to closed e.

metà.etymology: Continues Classical Latin mĕdĭĕtās, mĕdĭĕtātem ('middle, half', derived from mĕdĭus, 'middle'), via Old Italian medietade > meità > metà with apocope of the final syllable.

mezzanotte.etymology: Univerbation of mezza notte, continuing Latin mĕdĭa nŏx / mĕdĭam nŏctem ('middle of the night').
mezzanotte.notes: Like mezzogiorno, used without a definite article in time expressions: a mezzanotte ('at midnight'), è mezzanotte ('it's midnight').

mezzo.etymology: Continues Classical Latin mĕdĭus, mĕdĭum ('in the middle, half, medium'), with regular Tuscan evolution of intervocalic -di- before a vowel to the voiced dental affricate -zz- (/ddz/).

mezzogiorno.etymology: Transparent compound of mezzo ('half, middle', from Latin medius) + giorno ('day'), naming twelve noon (and, by extension, southern Italy where the midday sun stands).
mezzogiorno.notes: Capitalized il Mezzogiorno designates Southern Italy and the islands—just as French le Midi names Southern France—because the sun stands due south at noon.

mi.etymology: Continues Classical Latin mĭhī (contracted in colloquial Latin to mī, 'to me'), with raising of unstressed e to i in proclitic position as the first-person singular dative, accusative, and reflexive clitic pronoun ('me, to me, myself'); as the third note of the musical scale (E), from Mira gestorum in Guido of Arezzo's hymn Ut queant laxis.

history.meaning: me, to me, myself; mi, E (musical note)

miele.etymology: Continues Latin mel, stem mell- ('honey'), diphthongizing stressed open e to ie in open syllable.

cognates.meaning: learned Latin loan and distant Germanic cognate

miele.notes: Masculine in Italian (il miele) and French (le miel), whereas Spanish la miel became feminine.

migliore.etymology: Continues Classical Latin mĕlĭōrem (accusative of mĕlĭor, 'better', irregular comparative of bŏnus, 'good'), with regular Tuscan palatalization of -li- to -gli- (/ʎʎ/) and pretonic raising of e to i.

mille.etymology: Continues Classical Latin mīlle ('one thousand'; plural mīlia, whence Italian mila).

millefiori.etymology: Compound formed within Italian from mille ('thousand', < Latin mīlle) + fiori ('flowers', plural of fiore < Latin flōs, flōrem), literally 'a thousand flowers' (used for multifloral honey, millefiori glasswork, and floral fragrances).

millimetro.etymology: Learned metric compound borrowed via French millimètre, formed from Latin mīlle ('thousand', signifying 'one-thousandth') + metro ('meter', < Greek μέτρον, métron).

minore.etymology: Continues Classical Latin mĭnor, mĭnōrem ('smaller, lesser, younger', irregular comparative of parvus, 'small').

history.meaning: smaller, lesser, younger, minor; (with article) smallest

minuscolo.etymology: Learned borrowing from Classical Latin mĭnūscŭlus ('rather small, very small, tiny', diminutive of the comparative mĭnor, mĭnus, 'smaller, less'); in paleography and typography (lettera minuscola), 'lowercase'.

minuto.etymology: Continues Classical Latin mĭnūtus ('diminished, very small, fine, minute', past participle of mĭnuĕre, 'to make smaller'); as a unit of time or angle, from Medieval Latin pars minūta prīma ('first small division [one-sixtieth] of an hour or degree', translating Ptolemy's Greek).

history.meaning: first sixtieth part of an hour, minute

mio.etymology: Continues Classical Latin mĕus, mĕum ('my, mine'), with regular closure of stressed ĕ in hiatus before a back vowel to i (mĕum > *mĕo > mio).

miracolo.etymology: Semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin mīrāculum ('object of wonder, marvel, prodigy'), built from mīrārī ('to wonder at, marvel', from mīrus, 'wonderful') + instrumental/result suffix -culum. Its documented historical progression runs from Classical Latin mīrārī -> mīrāculum ('to marvel -> wonder, marvel') -> Late / Ecclesiastical Latin mīrāculum ('miracle') -> Italian miracolo ('miracle, marvel (fare miracoli = work wonders)'). Cross-linguistic cognates include fr miracle ('miracle'), es milagro ('miracle'), en miracle / mirror / marvel ('all share Latin mīrārī ('to look at in wonder')'); related Italian derivatives include miracoloso ('miraculous'), ammirare ('to admire'), mirare ('to gaze at, aim'). Fare miracoli is the warm everyday idiom for a remedy, rest, or cup of coffee working wonders.

cognates.meaning: all share Latin mīrārī ('to look at in wonder')

miracolo.notes: Fare miracoli is the warm everyday idiom for a remedy, rest, or cup of coffee working wonders.

mirtillo.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late and Medieval Latin myrtillus ('bilberry, little myrtle'), diminutive of Classical Latin myrtus ('myrtle shrub', < Ancient Greek mýrtos, μύρτος), named because bilberry/blueberry bushes bear small glossy leaves and dark blue-black berries resembling miniature myrtle berries.
mirtillo.notes: Covers both native European wild bilberries (mirtillo nero) and larger cultivated American blueberries (mirtillo gigante); mirtillo rosso is cranberry/lingonberry.

misterioso.etymology: Derived from mistero ('mystery, secret', learned continuation of Classical/Christian Latin mystērium < Ancient Greek μυστήριον, mystḗrion, 'secret rite, mystery') + the adjectival suffix -oso.

mistero.etymology: Learned borrowing from Classical/Ecclesiastical Latin mystērium ('secret rite, hidden truth'), from Ancient Greek mystḗrion ('secret rite', from mýstēs, 'initiate', and mýein, 'to close the eyes or lips'). Its documented historical progression runs from Ancient Greek mýein -> mystḗrion ('to close lips/eyes -> secret rite') -> Classical Latin mystērium ('secret, mystery') -> Italian mistero ('mystery, puzzle'). Cross-linguistic cognates include fr mystère ('mystery'), es misterio ('mystery'), en mystery ('enigma, puzzle'); related Italian derivatives include misterioso ('mysterious'), mistico ('mystical'). Greek mýein ('to keep one's lips closed') also lies behind English mute and myopia.
mistero.notes: Greek mýein ('to keep one's lips closed') also lies behind English mute and myopia.

misura.etymology: Continues Classical Latin mēnsūra ('measuring, measure, standard, limit', derived from mētīrī, 'to measure', past participle mēnsus), with regular Vulgar Latin reduction of -ns- to -s- and raising of pretonic e to i.

misurare.etymology: Continues Late Latin mēnsūrāre ('to measure'), denominative verb from Classical Latin mēnsūra ('measure'), with reduction of -ns- to -s-.

mito.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin mȳthus, from Ancient Greek μῦθος (mŷthos, 'word, speech, narrative, legendary tale, myth').

mobile.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin mōbĭlis ('easy to move, movable, changeable, nimble', contracted from *movĭbĭlis, from movēre, 'to move'); substantivized in the masculine (un mobile, pl. i mobili, from beni mobili, 'movable goods') for 'piece of furniture, furniture'.

moderno.etymology: Learned continuation of Late Latin mŏdĕrnus ('of the present time, recent, modern', attested from the 5th–6th centuries in Gelasius and Cassiodorus), derived from the Classical Latin adverb mŏdŏ ('just now, recently', originally ablative of mŏdus, 'by measure').

modo.etymology: Continues Classical Latin mŏdus, mŏdum ('measure, bound, rhythm, manner, way').

mollare.etymology: Deadjectival verb formed within Italian from molle ('soft, slack, pliable', inherited from Classical Latin mollis, -em); originally a maritime verb meaning 'to slacken or cast off a taut rope' (mollare gli ormeggi), whence 'to let go of, drop, quit'.

history.meaning: to slacken a cable, let go of a line
to let go, quit, give up, dump

cognates.meaning: to cast anchor (related Romance nautical family from mollis)

mollare.notes: In colloquial Italian, non mollare! means 'don't give up!', while mollare tutto or mollare qualcuno means walking away from a job or breaking up with a partner.

molto.etymology: Continues Classical Latin mŭltus, mŭltum ('much, many, abundant'; neuter mŭltum used adverbially, 'very, much'), with regular lowering of short Latin ŭ to closed o.

history.meaning: much, many, a lot of (adj./pron.); very, a lot (adv.)

momento.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin mōmentum ('movement, impulse; decisive weight on a scale; brief space of time, instant', contracted from *movĭmentum, from movēre, 'to move').

history.meaning: to move -> movement, brief interval, moment

moneta.etymology: Continues Latin monēta ('mint; coin'), from the temple of Iūnō Monēta on Rome's Capitoline Hill where silver coins were struck.

history.meaning: epithet of Juno at the Roman mint -> mint, coin

cognates.meaning: doublets via Old French and early West Germanic

moneta.notes: Hai moneta? ('Do you have small change / coins?') contrasts with banconote ('banknotes') and soldi ('money' in everyday speech).

montagna.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *montānĕa (neuter plural of montānĕus, 'of mountains', treated as a feminine singular collective), derived from Latin mōns, mŏntis.

rootFamily.gloss: mount (used in peak names: il Monte Bianco)

montagna.notes: Andare in montagna means 'to go to the mountains'; named peaks take monte instead (il Monte Rosa).

montare.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *montāre ('to go up a mountain, ascend, climb, mount, assemble'), denominative verb derived from Classical Latin mōns, montis ('mountain, hill').

morbido.etymology: Continues Classical Latin mŏrbĭdus ('sickly, diseased', from mŏrbus, 'disease'), which in pastoral and colloquial Latin shifted through 'languid, flaccid, tender, delicate' to the positive tactile sense 'soft, supple, smooth, mellow'.

morso.etymology: Continues Classical Latin mŏrsus, mŏrsum ('act of biting, bite, sting, horse's bit'), action noun and past participle of mŏrdēre ('to bite').

morte.etymology: Continues Classical Latin mŏrs, mŏrtem ('death'), from Proto-Indo-European *mértis (built on *mer-, 'to die').

mostrare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin mōnstrāre ('to point out, show, indicate, teach', derived from mōnstrum, 'divine omen, sign', from monēre, 'to warn, remind'), with regular Vulgar Latin reduction of -nstr- to -str-.

motivo.etymology: Learned continuation of Medieval Latin mōtīvus ('moving, impelling, serving as a cause or reason', derived from Classical Latin movēre, past participle mōtus, 'to move'); substantivized for an 'incentive, reason, motive' and in art/music for a 'recurring theme or motif'.

motore.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical/Late Latin mōtor, mōtōrem ('one that moves, mover', derived from movēre, past participle mōtus); specialized in modern engineering for a mechanical 'engine, motor'.

muovere.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *mŏvĕre, shifted to the third conjugation from Classical Latin mŏvēre ('to move, set in motion, stir'), with regular Tuscan diphthongization of stressed short ŏ to uo.

muro.etymology: Continues Classical Latin mūrus, mūrum ('city wall, stone wall, rampart').

muscolo.etymology: Learned/semi-learned continuation of Latin mūscŭlus ('little mouse; muscle', comparing the rippling of a flexed biceps under the skin to a mouse).

history.meaning: mouse -> little mouse; flexing muscle; sea mussel

muscolo.notes: Remarkably, on the Ligurian and Tuscan coast i muscoli also means 'mussels' (standard Southern/national cozze)—preserving the exact same dual sense that split into English 'muscle' and 'mussel'!

musica.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin mūsĭca (sc. ars, 'the art of music'), borrowed from Ancient Greek μουσική [τέχνη] (mousikḗ [tékhnē], 'art of the Muses, poetry and music', from Μοῦσα, Moûsa, 'Muse').

musicale.etymology: Learned continuation of Medieval Latin mūsĭcālis ('pertaining to music'), derived from Classical Latin mūsĭca ('music').

muto.etymology: Continues Classical Latin mūtus ('unable to speak, dumb, silent, mute'), of expressive origin (*mū-*, imitating an inarticulate murmur with closed lips).

nascere.etymology: Inherited from Vulgar Latin *nascĕre (active remodeling of Classical Latin deponent nāscī, archaic gnāscī, 'to be born, spring forth', from PIE root *ǵenh₁-, 'to beget, give birth'). Its irregular past participle nato continues Latin nātus directly.

cognates.meaning: coming into existence; innate (from the same Latin verb)

nascere.notes: Often used figuratively in Italian for melodies, friendships, or ideas that grow organically out of an earlier moment.

nascondere.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *inabscŏndĕre, reinforced compound of in- + Classical Latin abscŏndĕre ('to put away out of sight, conceal, hide', from abs- + condĕre, 'to put together, store away'), with apheresis of initial i-.

history.meaning: to put out of sight, hide

nascosto.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *inabscŏstus, analogical sigmatic past participle of *inabscŏndĕre (> nascondere, 'to hide', replacing Classical abscŏndĭtus / abscōnsus on the pattern of pōnĕre : pŏsĭtus > posto).

naso.etymology: Continues Classical Latin nāsus, nāsum ('nose; sense of smell, wit'), from the Proto-Indo-European root *néh₂s- ('nose').

nastro.etymology: Borrowed in the early Middle Ages from Gothic or Lombardic *nastilō ('strap, lace, ribbon, band for fastening clothing', cognate with Old High German nestila), with substitution of the ending and change of -l- to -r- after -st-.

naturale.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin nātūrālis ('by birth, according to nature, natural, unaffected'), derived from nātūra ('birth, character, nature', from nāscī, 'to be born').

naturalezza.etymology: Formed within Italian from naturale ('natural, unaffected', < Latin nātūrālis, from nātūra, 'nature, birth') + abstract quality suffix -ezza (< Latin -itia).
naturalezza.notes: Closely echoes the Renaissance Italian ideal of sprezzatura—doing something difficult with unforced, graceful ease (con naturalezza).

ne.etymology: Continues Classical Latin ĭnde ('from there, thence, thereof'), reduced in unstressed clitic position by apheresis of initial i- and assimilation/reduction of -nd- (> Old Italian ende / ne) to yield the partitive and genitive/ablative clitic pronoun ('of it, of them, some, from there').

history.meaning: of it, of them, some, any, about it, from there

neanche.etymology: Univerbation formed within Italian from né ('neither, nor', < Classical Latin nĕc) + anche ('also, even'), meaning 'not even, neither'.

negoziante.etymology: Substantivized present participle of negoziare ('to carry on trade, do business', < Classical Latin nĕgōtĭārī, derived from nĕgōtĭum, 'business'), designating a 'shopkeeper, merchant, trader'.

negozio.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin nĕgōtĭum ('business, occupation, affair, commercial transaction', negative compound of nĕc + ōtĭum, 'leisure', literally 'lack of leisure'), specialized in Italian for a retail 'shop, store'.

nel.etymology: Articulated preposition formed by the fusion of Old Italian in el / in lo ('in the', < Classical Latin ĭn ĭllō), with apheresis of initial i- yielding nel.

nella.etymology: Articulated preposition formed by the fusion of Old Italian in la ('in the', < Classical Latin ĭn ĭllam), with assimilation of -nl- to -ll- and apheresis of initial i-.

nelle.etymology: Articulated preposition formed by the fusion of Old Italian in le ('in the', < Classical Latin ĭn ĭllās / ĭllae), with assimilation of -nl- to -ll- and apheresis of initial i-.

nello.etymology: Articulated preposition formed by the fusion of Old Italian in lo ('in the', < Classical Latin ĭn ĭllum), with assimilation of -nl- to -ll- and apheresis of initial i-.

history.meaning: in the, into the (masculine singular before vowel/s+consonant/z)

nemmeno.etymology: Univerbation of the phrase né meno ('nor less, not even'), formed from né ('neither, nor', < Classical Latin nĕc) + meno ('less', < Classical Latin mĭnus), with regular syntactic gemination of -m-.

nero.etymology: Continues Classical Latin nĭger, nĭgrum ('black, dark, sable'), with regular lowering of short ĭ to closed e and vocalization/loss of -g- before -r- (*nĕgru > nero).

nessuno.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *ne ipse ūnus ('not even one'), compound of Classical Latin nĕ(c) + ipse ('himself, very') + ūnus ('one'), with palatal assimilation of -ps- (> Old Italian neuno / nissuno / nessuno).

neve.etymology: Continues Latin nĭx, nĭvem ('snow'), from the accusative nĭvem with regular Romance development ĭ > closed /e/.
neve.notes: In baking, montare gli albumi a neve means 'to whip egg whites until stiff like snow'.

niente.etymology: Exact Latin source debated; Treccani notes several proposals—most prominently Vulgar Latin *nec gentem ('not a soul/person') or *ne inde—with medieval Tuscan variants neente and neiente.
niente.notes: Di niente ('think nothing of it / you're welcome') is a polite everyday reply to grazie; after a verb, Italian uses negative concord: non ho visto niente ('I didn't see anything').

nipote.etymology: Continues Classical Latin nĕpōs, nĕpōtem ('grandson, descendant; in Late Latin also nephew/niece'), from Proto-Indo-European *népōts, preserving both senses ('grandchild' and 'nephew/niece') in Italian.

no.etymology: Continues Latin nōn in stressed standalone position, whereas unstressed proclitic position before a verb preserved the final nasal as non.
no.notes: Italian splits Latin nōn by stress: standalone or postposed no ('Vieni o no?') vs. unstressed preverbal non ('Non vengo').

noce.etymology: Continues Classical Latin nŭx, nŭcem ('walnut, nut; walnut tree'), with regular lowering of short Latin ŭ to closed o (feminine for the walnut fruit, masculine il noce for the tree and its timber).

noi.etymology: Continues Classical Latin nōs ('we, us'), with regular Italian vocalization of final -s in monosyllables to -i (compare voi < vōs, sei < sĕx).

noioso.etymology: Derived from noia ('annoyance, tedium, boredom', borrowed in the 13th century via Old Occitan enoja / noja from Late Latin inŏdĭa / phrase mihi in ŏdĭō est, 'it is hateful to me', from Classical Latin ŏdĭum, 'hatred, aversion') + the suffix -oso.

nome.etymology: Continues Classical Latin nōmen ('name, title, noun'), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁nómn̥ ('name'), with regular loss of final -n.

non.etymology: Continues Latin nōn (itself from Old Latin noenum, 'not one'). In Italian it stands directly before the verb phrase to negate a clause.

rootFamily.gloss: as well as, not to mention

non.notes: Always precedes the verb group (inclusively before object clitics: non lo so 'I don't know it'); negative singular tu imperatives use non + infinitive (non parlare!).

nonna.etymology: Continues Late Latin nŏnna ('revered elder woman, nun, grandmother'), an affectionate nursery reduplication.

history.meaning: revered elder woman, child's nurse, nun

cognates.meaning: early borrowing from Late Latin nonna

nonna.notes: While English and French kept Late Latin nonna in its monastic sense ('nun', Italian suora / monaca), Italian made nonna and nonno its warm everyday words for grandparents.

nonno.etymology: Continues Late Latin nonnus (originally a respectful address to an elder or monk), which replaced classical avus as the everyday word for grandfather.
nonno.notes: With kinship singulars without adjectives, Italian drops the definite article before possessives (mio nonno), but keeps it in the plural (i miei nonni, 'my grandparents').

nono.etymology: Continues Classical Latin nōnus ('ninth', contracted from Old Latin *novenos, ordinal numeral derived from nŏvem, 'nine').

nord.etymology: Borrowed via Old French nord (or maritime Spanish/Portuguese norte) from Old English norþ / Frankish *norþ ('north'), ultimately from Proto-Germanic *nurþrą, replacing Classical Latin septentriōnēs in everyday navigation. Its documented historical progression runs from Proto-Germanic / Old English *nurþrą / norþ ('north') -> Old French nord ('north (maritime compass point)') -> Italian nord ('north'). Cross-linguistic cognates include fr nord ('north'), es norte ('north'), de Nord / Norden ('north'); related Italian derivatives include nordico ('northern, Nordic'), nordest ('north-east'), nordovest ('north-west'). All four modern Italian cardinal directions—nord, sud, est, ovest—entered Romance seafaring vocabulary from Germanic!
nord.notes: All four modern Italian cardinal directions—nord, sud, est, ovest—entered Romance seafaring vocabulary from Germanic!

normale.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin normālis ('made according to the carpenter's square, right-angled, regular'), derived from norma ('carpenter's square, rule, pattern, standard').

history.meaning: carpenter's square, rule -> made according to rule, regular

normalissimo.etymology: Absolute superlative formed in Italian from normale ('normal, regular', learned borrowing from Classical Latin normālis, 'made according to the carpenter's square', from norma, 'carpenter's square, rule') + the superlative suffix -issimo (< -issimus).
normalissimo.notes: Italian speakers attach -issimo even to logically non-gradable adjectives like normale, vero (verissimo), and giusto (giustissimo) for warm conversational reassurance ('perfectly normal!').

nostro.etymology: Continues Classical Latin nŏster, nŏstrum ('our, ours'), derived from nōs ('we, us').

nota.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin nŏta ('mark, sign, written character, memorandum, critical mark'), related to nōscĕre ('to come to know', past participle nōtus); in medieval music, applied to a written musical sign or pitch.

notare.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin nŏtāre ('to mark, designate with a mark, observe, write down'), denominative verb from nŏta ('mark, sign').

history.meaning: mark, sign -> to mark, observe, take note

notizia.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin nōtĭtĭa ('being known, celebrity, acquaintance, knowledge, notion, list'), derived from nōtus ('known', past participle of nōscĕre); in Italian specialized as 'piece of news, information, notice'.

notte.etymology: Continues Classical Latin nŏx, nŏctem ('night'), from Proto-Indo-European *nókʷts ('night'), with regular assimilation of the -ct- cluster to geminate -tt-.

nove.etymology: Continues Classical Latin nŏvem ('nine'), from Proto-Indo-European *h₁néwn̥ ('nine'), with regular loss of final -m.

novellina.etymology: Feminine of novellino ('newly arrived, inexperienced, beginner', diminutive of novello < Classical Latin nŏvĕllus, 'new, young, fresh', itself a diminutive of nŏvus, 'new').

nudo.etymology: Continues Classical Latin nūdus ('naked, bare, uncovered, unadorned'), from Proto-Indo-European *nogʷódʰos ('naked').

numero.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin nŭmĕrus ('number, count, quantity, musical measure').

nuovo.etymology: Continues Classical Latin nŏvus, nŏvum ('new, young, fresh, recent'), from Proto-Indo-European *néwos, with regular Tuscan diphthongization of stressed short ŏ in an open syllable to uo.

o.etymology: Continues Classical Latin aut ('or'), with regular monophthongization of Latin au to o and loss of final -t before consonants (while retaining euphonic -d in od before vowels).

obbligare.etymology: Semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin obligāre ('to bind around, tie up; to bind morally or legally'), composed of ob- ('toward, around') + ligāre ('to tie, bind'), showing regular central-Italian gemination of voiced -b- before liquid -l- (-bl- > -bbl-).

morphemes.meaning: around, toward (< Latin ob- with geminated b)

history.meaning: to bind fast, place under obligation

rootFamily.gloss: to tie, bind (popular reflex of ligāre)

obbligare.notes: Spelled with double bb in Italian (like pubblico and repubblica); takes preposition a before an infinitive (obbligare qualcuno a fare qualcosa).

occhiale.etymology: Derived from occhio ('eye', < Latin oculus); plural gli occhiali ('eyeglasses') was coined in late-thirteenth-century Italy where wearable spectacles were first crafted.
occhiale.notes: Wearable spectacles were invented in northern/central Italy around 1285–1290 (celebrated in a 1306 sermon in Florence by Giordano da Pisa), giving rise to plural gli occhiali.

occhiata.etymology: Derived within Italian from occhio ('eye', < Latin ŏcŭlus) + the suffix -ata, designating a 'quick look, glance, gaze'.

occhio.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin ŏclus, syncopated from Classical Latin ŏcŭlus ('eye', originally diminutive of *ŏkʷ-, 'eye'), with regular Tuscan evolution of intervocalic -cl- to geminate palatal -cchi- (/kkj/).

occupare.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin occŭpāre ('to seize, take possession of, fill up, employ'), compound of ob- ('over, against') + root of capĕre ('to take, seize').

history.meaning: to take possession of, seize, busy

occupato.etymology: Continues Classical Latin occŭpātus ('taken possession of, engaged, busy, employed'), past participle of occŭpāre ('to occupy, busy').

history.meaning: to take up, engage -> busy, engaged, occupied
busy, occupied, taken (of a seat or phone line)

odore.etymology: Continues Latin odōr, odōrem ('smell, scent, fragrance'), cognate with Greek ὄζω (ózō, 'to smell').

history.meaning: smell, scent; (pl. odori) aromatic kitchen herbs

odore.notes: Neutral or pleasant in Italian (unlike English 'odour'): un buon odore di caffè, and plural gli odori in cooking means a bundle of carrot, celery, onion, parsley, and rosemary.

offerta.etymology: Substantivised feminine past participle of offrire ('to offer', < Vulgar Latin *offerīre for Classical offerre, from ob- + ferre, 'to bring before, present'). Its documented historical progression runs from Vulgar Latin *offerīre -> *offerta ('to offer -> thing offered') -> Italian offerta ('offer, bid, special sale price (in offerta)'). Cross-linguistic cognates include fr offre / offerte ('offer / offered'), es oferta ('offer, bargain'), en offer ('proposal, special price'); related Italian derivatives include offrire ('to offer, treat'), offerente ('bidder'). In Italian shops and markets, in offerta means 'on sale / at a bargain price'.

history.meaning: offer, bid, special sale price (in offerta)

offerta.notes: In Italian shops and markets, in offerta means 'on sale / at a bargain price'.

offrire.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *offerīre, regularized fourth-conjugation verb from Classical Latin offerre ('to bring before, present, offer', compound of ob- + ferre, 'to bear, bring'), with syncope of the unstressed vowel.

oggetto.etymology: Learned borrowing from Medieval/Scholastic Latin obiectum ('something thrown or placed before the mind or senses, object'), substantivized neuter past participle of Classical Latin obĭcĕre ('to throw before, present', from ob- + iacĕre).

oggi.etymology: Continues Classical Latin hŏdĭē ('today', contracted from hōc dĭē, 'on this day'), with regular loss of initial h- and Tuscan evolution of intervocalic -di- before a vowel to geminate palatal -ggi- (/ddʒ/).

ogni.etymology: Continues Classical Latin ŏmnis, ŏmnes ('all, every'), with regular assimilation/palatalization in proclitic position of -mn- before final -i (< -ēs) to -gn- (/ɲɲ/, Old Italian ogne > ogni).

ognuno.etymology: Univerbation of Old Italian ogni uno ('each one, every single one'), from ogni ('every', < Classical Latin omnis, 'all, every') + uno ('one', < Latin ūnus). Its documented historical progression runs from Classical Latin omnis + ūnus ('every + one') -> Old Italian ogni uno ('each one') -> Italian ognuno / ognuna ('everyone, each one'). Cross-linguistic cognates include fr chacun ('each one (parallel compound with un)'), en everyone ('exact structural parallel ('every' + 'one')'); related Italian derivatives include ogni ('every, each'), uno ('one'), qualcuno ('someone'). Used only in the singular: ognuno (masculine/general) and ognuna (feminine, e.g., ognuna delle sedie).
ognuno.notes: Used only in the singular: ognuno (masculine/general) and ognuna (feminine, e.g., ognuna delle sedie).

oh.etymology: Primary vocalic interjection of surprise, wonder, pleasure, or appeal, continuing Classical Latin ō / oh.

ok.etymology: Twentieth-century international borrowing from American English O.K. / okay, used in spoken Italian as an informal check or agreement.
ok.notes: Pronounced /oˈkɛj/ in Italian and used constantly in casual conversation alongside native va bene and d'accordo.

oliare.etymology: Denominative verb built in Italian from olio ('oil', < Classical Latin oleum, borrowed from Ancient Greek ἔλαιον, élaion, 'olive oil') + first-conjugation verbal suffix -are.
oliare.notes: Used both for oiling iron gate hinges and for lightly oiling a baking tin or wooden chopping board.

olio.etymology: Continues Latin ŏlĕum ('olive oil'), an ancient Mediterranean word borrowed alongside Greek ἔλαιον (élaion).

cognates.meaning: borrowed via Old Northern French oli

olio.notes: At the Italian table, l'olio without qualification always means extra-virgin olive oil (olio extravergine d'oliva).

oliva.etymology: Continues Latin ŏlīva ('olive fruit; olive tree'), early borrowing from archaic Greek *ἐλαίϝα (*elaíwa).
oliva.notes: Feminine l'oliva is the fruit, while masculine l'olivo (or l'ulivo, as in Domenica delle Palme olive branches) is the tree.

oltre.etymology: Continues Classical Latin ŭltrā ('beyond, on the further side, more than'), with regular lowering of short Latin ŭ to closed o and change of final -a to -e (via Old Italian oltra / oltre, influenced by adverbs in -e).

ombra.etymology: Continues Latin ŭmbra ('shadow, shade'), with regular Tuscan opening of tonic short ŭ to closed /o/.

history.meaning: shadow, shade; (Venetian) small glass of wine

cognates.meaning: from Italian ombrello and French ombrage

ombra.notes: In Venice, un'ombra (de vin) famously means a small glass of wine—traditionally poured by vendors who moved their stalls around Piazza San Marco following the cool shadow of the Campanile.

onestamente.etymology: Formed in Italian from the feminine singular onesta of onesto ('honest, honorable', continuing Classical Latin honestus 'held in honor, respectable', from honōs / honor 'honor, esteem') plus the Romance manner suffix -mente (grammaticalised from Latin ablative mente 'with a ... mind').

morphemes.meaning: adverbial manner suffix (< Latin mente 'in mind')

onestamente.notes: Like English honestly, it works both inside the clause ('to behave fairly') and at the start of a sentence to signal candor (Onestamente, preferisco così).

onesto.etymology: Continues Classical Latin hŏnĕstus ('regarded with honor, honorable, respectable, upright'), derived from hŏnos / hŏnor ('honor, esteem').

oplà.etymology: Expressive exclamation accompanying a jump, lift, or sudden nimble movement, borrowed from or parallel to French hop là! (from the interjection hop! + là, 'there!').

oppure.etymology: Univerbation formed within Italian from o ('or', < Classical Latin aut) + pure ('yet, also, even', < Latin pūrē), with regular syntactic gemination of -p-.

ora.etymology: Continues Classical Latin hōra ('hour, time of day, season'), borrowed from Ancient Greek ὥρα (hṓra, 'season, time of day, hour'); used both as the noun 'hour' and (by ellipsis of in questa ora) as the temporal adverb 'now'.

orario.etymology: Learned continuation of Medieval/Late Latin hōrārius ('pertaining to the hours', derived from Classical Latin hōra, 'hour'); substantivized in the masculine (l'orario) for 'timetable, schedule, working/opening hours'.

ordinare.etymology: Continues Latin ōrdĭnāre ('to set in rows, arrange, command'), built on ōrdō, ōrdĭnis ('row, order').

history.meaning: row, rank -> to set in order, command
to put in order; to order (food/goods); command

ordinare.notes: Used at cafés and trattorias just like English 'to order' (possiamo ordinare? 'may we order?').

ordinato.etymology: Continues Classical Latin ōrdĭnātus ('arranged in rows, set in order, regular, orderly'), past participle of ōrdĭnāre ('to set in order, arrange, command', from ōrdō, ōrdĭnis, 'row, rank, order').

ordine.etymology: Continues Latin ōrdinem (accusative of ōrdō, 'row, arrangement, command'), originally a weaving term for threads in a loom.

history.meaning: row of threads on a loom; rank, order

ordine.notes: Mettere in ordine means 'to tidy up', while fuori d'ordine is not used for broken machines—Italian says fuori servizio or guasto.

orecchio.etymology: Continues Latin aurĭcŭla (diminutive of auris, 'ear') via masculine reshaping *aurĭcŭlum, with au- > o- and -cl- > -cchi-.

cognates.meaning: learned Latin borrowing and Indo-European cognate

orecchio.notes: Both masculine l'orecchio (pl. gli orecchi / le orecchie) and feminine l'orecchia exist; figurative phrases like avere buon orecchio ('to have a good musical ear') always use masculine.

organizzare.etymology: Learned continuation of Medieval/Late Latin organĭzāre ('to furnish with organs, play the organ; arrange systematically'), from Ancient Greek ὀργανίζειν (organízein, derived from ὄργανον, órganon, 'instrument, tool, organ'), reinforced in modern senses by French organiser.

ormai.etymology: Univerbation of the adverbial phrase or mai (also omai, 'now more, by now'), formed from ora ('now', < Latin hōra) + mai ('ever, more', < Latin măgis).

history.meaning: by now, at this point, now

oro.etymology: Continues Classical Latin aurum ('gold'), from Proto-Indo-European *h₂é-h₂us-o- ('glowing dawn-colored metal'), with regular monophthongization of Latin au to open o.

orologiaio.etymology: Derived with agent suffix -aio (< Latin -ārius) from orologio ('clock, watch', < Latin hōrolŏgĭum < Greek ὡρολόγιον, 'hour-teller').
orologiaio.notes: Like fornaio ('baker'), libraio ('bookseller'), and benzinaio ('petrol-station attendant'), Tuscan -aio (< Latin -ārius) is Italian's classic trade and craft suffix.

orologio.etymology: Continues Latin hōrologium (from Ancient Greek hōrológion, 'hour-teller', from hṓra 'hour' + légein 'to tell').
orologio.notes: Unlike French (horloge vs. montre) and English ('clock' vs. 'watch'), Italian uses un orologio for both a wall clock and a wristwatch.

ospitalità.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin hospĭtālĭtās, hospĭtālĭtātem ('hospitality, friendliness to guests'), derived from hospĭtālis ('relating to a guest or host', from hospĕs, hospĭtis).

ospitare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin hospĭtārī ('to lodge as a guest'), denominative verb from hospĕs, hospĭtis ('host; guest, stranger'), shifting in Italian to the transitive sense 'to host, receive as a guest, accommodate'.

ospite.etymology: Continues Latin hospitem (accusative of hospes), which already denoted both partners of hospitality—the host who welcomes and the guest who is welcomed.

history.meaning: host; guest; stranger bound by reciprocity

cognates.meaning: Old French borrowing and native Indo-European cognate (*ghóstis)

ospite.notes: Preserves ancient Roman xenia/hospitalitas reciprocity: l'ospite can mean either the guest visiting a home/TV show or the host receiving them, clarified by context.

ottanta.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *octanta, contracted from Classical Latin octōgintā ('eighty', derived from octō, 'eight'), with regular assimilation of -ct- to -tt-.

ottava.etymology: Feminine substantivisation of ottavo (< Latin octāvus, 'eighth', from ŏctō, 'eight'), short for ottava corda or ottava nota.
ottava.notes: Famous in both music (un'ottava sopra, 'an octave higher') and Renaissance verse (ottava rima, the ABABABCC stanza of Ariosto and Tasso).

ottimo.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin ŏptĭmus ('best, very good', irregular superlative of bŏnus, 'good', related to ops, 'power, resources'), with regular assimilation of -pt- to -tt-.

otto.etymology: Continues Classical Latin ŏctō ('eight'), from Proto-Indo-European *oḱtōw ('eight'), with regular assimilation of the -ct- cluster to geminate -tt-.

ottone.etymology: Derived from Old Italian latone ('brass', with rebracketing of initial l- as the definite article: l'otone > ottone), borrowed from Arabic لَاطُون (lāṭūn, 'copper, brass', itself from Turkish altun, 'gold, copper').

ovunque.etymology: Univerbation modeled on Classical Latin ŭbīcŭmque ('wherever'), formed in Old Italian from ove ('where', < Latin ŭbĭ) + unque ('ever', < Latin ŭnquam).

pacchetto.etymology: Diminutive of pacco ('package, parcel, bundle', borrowed via Dutch/Germanic *pak from Middle Low German or French paquet) formed with the suffix -etto.

pace.etymology: Continues Classical Latin pāx, pācem ('peace, treaty, tranquility, calm'), built on the Proto-Indo-European root *peh₂ǵ- ('to fasten, fix, agree upon a pact').

pagare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin pācāre ('to make peaceful, pacify, appease', derived from pāx, pācis, 'peace'), which in Late/Vulgar Latin commercial usage came to mean 'to appease or satisfy a creditor by settling a debt, pay'.

pagina.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin pāgĭna ('column of writing on a papyrus roll, leaf, page', originally 'trellis of vines fastened together', from pangĕre, 'to fasten, fix').

history.meaning: to fasten -> column of writing, page

pagnotta.etymology: Formed on pane ('bread', < Latin pānis) with diminutive/round-shape suffix -otta (*paniotta), denoting a single round loaf.
pagnotta.notes: Colloquially guadagnarsi la pagnotta ('to earn one's loaf') means 'to earn one's daily living'.

paio.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *pārium ('a pair of equal things'), substantivized neuter from Classical Latin pār, păris ('equal, matching; a pair', plural păria, preserved in the feminine plural le paia), with regular Tuscan reduction of -ri- to -i-.

palazzo.etymology: From Latin Palātium (the Palatine Hill in Rome, site of the imperial residences), broadening in Italian cities to mean any multi-storey masonry town building.

history.meaning: the Palatine Hill in Rome; imperial residence
palace, historic town mansion; apartment building

cognates.meaning: via Old French and directly from Italian

rootFamily.gloss: small low-rise apartment block or villa

palazzo.notes: Important everyday meaning: in modern Italian cities, un palazzo does not have to be royal—it is the ordinary word for any multi-storey apartment or office building!

palmo.etymology: Continues Classical Latin palmus ('palm of the hand; hand-span measure'), derived from palma ('flat of the hand; palm tree, whose leaves spread like fingers', from PIE *pḷh₂-meh₂, 'flat surface').

rootFamily.gloss: palm tree; palm of the hand

palmo.notes: Portare qualcuno in palmo di mano ('to carry someone on the palm of one's hand') means to cherish and praise them warmly.

pane.etymology: Continues Latin pānem (accusative of pānis, 'bread'), shared with compagno ('companion', literally one who shares bread).

cognates.meaning: via Old French paneterie and compagnon

pane.notes: Buono come il pane ('as good as bread') is one of Italian's warmest praises for a kindhearted person.

panico.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin pānĭcus, from Ancient Greek πανικός (panikós, 'of the god Pan', as in πανικὸς φόβος, panikòs phóbos, 'sudden groundless terror attributed to the woodland god Pan').

history.meaning: sudden terror caused by the god Pan

panino.etymology: Diminutive of pane ('bread', < Classical Latin pānis, pānem) formed with the suffix -ino, designating a small bread roll or a filled sandwich.

pannello.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *pannĕllus ('small piece of cloth, patch', diminutive of Classical Latin pannus, 'cloth, rag'), reinforced in architectural and carpentry senses ('wooden or metal panel') by Old French panel / French panneau.

history.meaning: piece of cloth -> small cloth, panel
piece of cloth, saddle pad, wooden panel

panno.etymology: Continues Classical Latin pannus ('piece of cloth, garment, rag, cloth wrap').

history.meaning: cloth, cleaning rag, woolen fabric; clothes (pl. panni)

paragrafo.etymology: Learned borrowing from Late Latin parăgrăphus, from Ancient Greek παράγραφος (parágraphos, short for παράγραφος γραμμή, 'marginal stroke written beside a text to mark a break in sense or speaker', from παραγράφειν, 'to write beside').

history.meaning: marginal mark indicating a section break

parcheggiare.etymology: 20th-century denominative verb from parcheggio ('parking, parking lot'), adapted from English parking / to park (itself ultimately from Old French parc, 'enclosed ground where military vehicles and horses were stationed').

history.meaning: to leave a vehicle in a designated space

parete.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *parētem (with shift from -iĕ- to closed -ē-), from Classical Latin părĭēs, părĭĕtem ('wall of a room or house, partition wall', as opposed to mūrus, 'outer defensive/structural wall'), shifting from masculine to feminine gender.

parlare.etymology: Continues Christian Late Latin parabolāre ('to speak in parables, converse', from Greek parabolḗ), which became the everyday word for speaking in Italian and French.
parlare.notes: While Spanish and Portuguese turned Late Latin fābulārī into hablar / falar, Gallo-Romance and Italian turned Christian parabolāre into parler and parlare.

parola.etymology: Continues Christian Late Latin parăbŏla ('comparison, parable, speech, word of Christ', borrowed from Ancient Greek παραβολή, parabolḗ, 'comparison, allegory'), which via syncopated Vulgar Latin *paraula (> parola) displaced Classical verbum across most of Romance.

parte.etymology: Continues Classical Latin pars, partem ('part, portion, share, side, direction, role').

partire.etymology: Continues Classical Latin partīrī / partīre ('to divide, share, distribute', derived from pars, partis, 'part'), which in Late/Vulgar Latin reflexive/intransitive usage (sē partīre ab, 'to separate oneself from') came to mean 'to depart, leave, set out'.

passaggio.etymology: Formed in Old Italian (reinforced by Old French passage) from passare ('to pass, step across', < Vulgar Latin *passāre, from passus, 'step, pace') + action/place noun suffix -aggio (< Latin -āticum via Gallo-Romance).
passaggio.notes: Di passaggio means 'passing through briefly', while in music un passaggio is a bridge or transition linking two sections.

passare.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *passāre ('to take steps, walk through, cross, pass'), denominative verb derived from Classical Latin passus ('step, pace').

history.meaning: to pass, go by, spend (time), hand over

passo.etymology: Continues Classical Latin passus, passum ('step, stride, pace, footprint, mountain pass', originally 'stretching out of the legs in walking', from pandĕre, 'to spread, stretch out', past participle passus).

history.meaning: to stretch out -> stride, step, pace

pasta.etymology: Continues Late Latin pasta ('kneaded dough, paste'), from Greek πάστη (pástē, 'barley porridge, salted meal').

cognates.meaning: doublets via Old French and modern Italian

pasta.notes: Beyond spaghetti and rigatoni, una pasta (pl. le paste) at a café or bakery also means an individual cream-filled pastry, and pasta frolla is shortcrust dough.

pasticceria.etymology: Derived from pasticciere ('pastry chef') / pasticcio ('pie, pastry', < Vulgar Latin *pastīcium, from Late Latin pasta, 'dough, paste', < Ancient Greek παστά, 'barley porridge') + workshop/craft suffix -eria.

cognates.meaning: pastry shop, pastry-making (borrowed from Italian in the Renaissance!)

pasticceria.notes: French pâtisserie was actually modeled on Renaissance Italian pasticceria when Italian pastry chefs traveled to the French court in the 16th century.

paura.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *pavōra, originally a collective neuter plural reshaped from Classical Latin păvor, păvōrem ('trembling, dread, fear, panic', derived from păvēre, 'to tremble with fear, be terrified'), with loss of intervocalic -v-.

pavimento.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin păvīmentum ('hard floor of rammed earth, stone, or mosaic tiles'), derived from păvīre ('to beat down, ram, tread flat').

history.meaning: to ram, beat flat -> rammed or tiled floor

pazienza.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin pătĭĕntĭa ('endurance, forbearance, patience'), derived from pătĭēns, present participle of pătī ('to suffer, bear, endure').

pazzia.etymology: Formed within Italian from pazzo ('mad, crazy') + the stressed abstract suffix -ia; pazzo itself is most plausibly traced to Vulgar Latin *patius (back-formed from Classical Latin patiēns, 'suffering, mentally afflicted', from patī, 'to suffer').
pazzia.notes: Used hyperbolically in everyday speech (è una pazzia!, 'it is sheer madness!') for reckless schedules or decisions.

pedale.etymology: Continues Classical Latin pĕdālis ('of a foot, foot-long, pertaining to the foot', derived from pēs, pĕdis, 'foot'); substantivized in Italian (whence French pédale and English pedal) for an organ, piano, or bicycle 'foot lever, pedal'.

peggio.etymology: Continues Classical Latin pĕĭus ('worse', neuter comparative of mălus, 'bad', and comparative adverb of mălē, 'badly'), with regular Tuscan evolution of intervocalic -i- (/j/) to geminate palatal -ggi- (/ddʒ/).

pelle.etymology: Continues Classical Latin pĕllis, pĕllem ('animal hide, pelt, skin'), from Proto-Indo-European *pelnis ('skin, film').

penna.etymology: Continues Classical Latin pĕnna ('feather, wing; in Late Latin, quill pen for writing'), from Old Latin petna (< Proto-Indo-European *péth₂r̥ / *pet-neh₂, from *peth₂-, 'to fly').

pennellata.etymology: Derived within Italian from pennello ('paintbrush', < Classical Latin pēnĭcĭllum / pēnĭcĕllus, 'painter's brush, small tail', double diminutive of pēnis, 'tail') + the single-action suffix -ata.

pennello.etymology: Continues Latin pēnicĭllus ('small tail; painter's tuft brush'), double diminutive of pēnis ('tail').

cognates.meaning: from Old French pincel and Latin pēnicillus

rootFamily.gloss: to brush on (glaze, egg wash, paint)

pennello.notes: English 'pencil' originally meant a fine camel-hair paintbrush before shifting to graphite sticks; Italian pennello kept the brush meaning (calzare a pennello 'to fit like a glove / as if painted on').

pensare.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin pēnsāre ('to weigh carefully, ponder, consider', frequentative of pĕndĕre, 'to weigh'), whereas the inherited popular development yielded pesare ('to weigh').

history.meaning: to weigh -> to weigh in the mind, ponder

pentola.etymology: Tuscan word attested since the 13th century for a deep earthenware or metal cooking pot, traditionally traced to Vulgar Latin *pinctula or a Mediterranean/Etruscan vessel name with diminutive suffix -ola.
pentola.notes: Sapere cosa bolle in pentola ('to know what is boiling in the pot') is the classic Italian idiom for knowing what is secretly being planned.

per.etymology: Continues Classical Latin pĕr ('through, by means of, during, for the sake of'), which in Italian absorbed the functions of Classical prō ('for, on behalf of, in exchange for').

history.meaning: for, through, by, in order to

perbacco.etymology: Univerbation of the mild euphemistic exclamation per Bacco! ('by Bacchus!', invoking the Roman god of wine Bacchus in place of sacred religious names).

perché.etymology: Univerbation of the phrase per che ('for what [reason/cause]', from per < Latin pĕr + che < Latin quid / quod), functioning as both 'why?' and 'because, so that'.

history.meaning: for what reason / for the reason that

perdere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin pĕrdĕre ('to destroy, ruin, waste, lose irrevocably'), compound of per- ('through, to destruction') + dăre / *-dĕre ('to put').

perfetto.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin pĕrfĕctus ('thoroughly made, completed, finished, accomplished, faultless'), past participle of pĕrfĭcĕre ('to bring to completion', from per- + facĕre, 'to make, do').

history.meaning: to complete thoroughly -> completed, flawless, perfect

perfino.etymology: Univerbation of the prepositional phrase per fino ('up to the end, even'), formed from per ('through, for') + fino ('until, up to', < Latin fīnis).

pericolo.etymology: Continues Classical Latin perīculum ('trial, attempt, risk, danger'), formed from the archaic verbal root *perī- (seen in experīrī, 'to try, test', and perītus, 'experienced', from PIE *per-, 'to try, risk, cross over') + instrument/means suffix -culum.

cognates.meaning: danger (with metathesis of r and l)

pericolo.notes: In Latin, perīculum originally meant 'a trial or experiment', before narrowing to the risk involved in trying something daring.

permesso.etymology: Continues Classical Latin pĕrmĭssus ('allowed, granted', past participle of pĕrmĭttĕre, and fourth-declension action noun pĕrmĭssus, 'leave, permission'); also used as a polite formula when entering a room or passing through ('excuse me, may I come in?').

history.meaning: to let through, allow -> allowed; permission
permission, permit; excuse me / may I come in?

permettere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin pĕrmĭttĕre ('to let pass through, give leave, allow, permit'), compound of per- ('through') + mĭttĕre ('to let go, send').

perno.etymology: Continues Latin pĕrna ('ham, leg, wooden tenon or pivot shaped like a haunch') via Vulgar Latin *pĕrnum.

history.meaning: ham, leg; wooden tenon or pivot

rootFamily.gloss: to hinge or center (an argument) upon

perno.notes: Fare perno su qualcosa means 'to pivot on / rely on something as a cornerstone'.

persiana.etymology: Substantivized feminine of the adjective persiano ('Persian', < Latin Persiānus), modeled in the 18th century on French persienne ('louvered window shutter with slanted slats', so named because such ventilated blinds were associated with Persia and the Near East).

persino.etymology: Univerbation of Old Italian per sino ('even, right up to'), variant of perfino formed from per + sino ('up to, until', altered from fino by crossing with segno < Latin signum).

persona.etymology: Continues Classical Latin persōna ('actor's theatrical mask; dramatic character, role; legal person, individual human being'), probably borrowed into Latin from Etruscan φersu ('masked figure').

però.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin per hōc ('for this reason, therefore', compound of Classical Latin pĕr + ablative hōc); in Old Italian it meant 'therefore' (preserved in però che), before shifting through negative clauses to the adversative sense 'however, yet, but'.

pesante.etymology: Participial adjective from the present participle of pesare ('to weigh, be heavy', < Vulgar Latin *pēsāre < Classical pēnsāre).

pesare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin pēnsāre ('to weigh out, counterbalance', frequentative of pĕndĕre, 'to weigh'), with regular Vulgar Latin reduction of the -ns- cluster to -s- (*pēsāre; compare learned pensare, 'to think').

peso.etymology: Continues Classical Latin pēnsum ('portion of wool weighed out to a spinner for a day's work; weight', neuter past participle of pĕndĕre, 'to weigh'), with regular Vulgar Latin reduction of -ns- to -s- (*pēsum).

piacere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin plăcēre ('to please, be agreeable, be welcome'), with regular Tuscan palatalization of initial pl- to pi- (/pj/); substantivized in the masculine (il piacere) for 'pleasure, favor' and as the polite greeting 'pleased to meet you'.

history.meaning: to be pleasing, like (verb); pleasure, favor, nice to meet you (noun)

piacevole.etymology: Adjective formed in Old Italian from piacere ('to please', < Classical Latin plăcēre) + the suffix -evole (< Latin -ĭbĭlis), meaning 'pleasant, agreeable, enjoyable'.

pianerottolo.etymology: Derived within Tuscan from piano ('flat level, floor', < Latin plānus) with the interfix -er- and diminutive suffix -ottolo, designating the flat 'landing' at the top of a flight of stairs.

piangere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin plangĕre ('to strike, beat the breast in mourning, lament aloud'), with regular Tuscan palatalization of initial pl- to pi- (/pj/), which in Italian displaced Classical flēre ('to weep').

history.meaning: to beat the breast in grief, lament

piano.etymology: Continues Classical Latin plānus ('flat, level, even, clear, low-voiced'), with regular Tuscan palatalization of initial pl- to pi- (/pj/); used as an adjective ('flat, slow, soft'), adverb ('slowly, quietly'), and noun ('flat surface, story/floor of a building, plan', and by clipping from pianoforte, 'piano').

history.meaning: flat, slow, quiet; floor/story, plan, piano

pianoforte.etymology: Shortened from gravicembalo col piano e col forte ('harpsichord with soft and loud'), coined in Florence by Bartolomeo Cristofori around 1700 for his hammer-action keyboard instrument.

history.form: gravicembalo col piano e col forte

pianoforte.notes: Unlike plucked harpsichords, Bartolomeo Cristofori's Medici-court invention responded to finger touch with soft (piano) and loud (forte) dynamics—giving the world its name for the piano.

pianta.etymology: Continues Classical Latin planta ('sprout, shoot, cutting for propagation; sole of the foot'), with regular Tuscan evolution of initial pl- to pi- (/pj/), uniting the botanical sense ('plant') and the architectural/cartographic sense ('floor plan, map', originally the 'footprint' of a building).

history.meaning: plant shoot; sole of the foot
plant, tree; floor plan, map; sole of the foot

pianterreno.etymology: Univerbation of the nominal phrase piano terreno ('ground-level storey'), combining piano ('flat level, floor', < Latin plānum) + terreno ('of the earth/ground', < Latin terrēnus, from terra). Its documented historical progression runs from Early Modern Italian piano terreno ('storey level with the street') -> Italian pianterreno ('ground floor'). Cross-linguistic cognates include fr rez-de-chaussée ('ground floor (street-level equivalent)'), es planta baja ('ground floor'); related Italian derivatives include piano ('floor, storey; flat'), terreno ('ground, plot of land'), terra ('earth, ground (also piano terra)'). Interchangeable with piano terra; in Italian buildings, il primo piano is always one flight above il pianterreno.
pianterreno.notes: Interchangeable with piano terra; in Italian buildings, il primo piano is always one flight above il pianterreno.

piantina.etymology: Diminutive of pianta ('plant; floor plan, map', < Classical Latin planta) formed with the suffix -ina, designating both a 'young seedling, small potted plant' and a 'floor plan, street map'.

history.meaning: small plant, seedling; floor plan, layout, map

piattino.etymology: Diminutive of piatto ('plate, dish', < Late Latin *plattus) formed with the suffix -ino, designating a small plate or teacup 'saucer'.

piatto.etymology: Continues Vulgar/Late Latin *plattus ('flat, level'), borrowed from Ancient Greek πλατύς (platýs, 'broad, flat'), with regular Tuscan palatalization of initial pl- to pi- (/pj/); substantivized in the masculine (il piatto) for a flat serving 'plate, dish, course of a meal'.

piazza.etymology: Continues Latin platĕa ('broad street, open courtyard'), borrowed from Greek πλατεῖα (plateîa, 'wide way'), with regular Italian development of -tj- > -zz- and pl- > pi-.

cognates.meaning: triple borrowing via French, Spanish, and Italian

piazza.notes: Shows regular Italian pl- > pi- and -tj- > -zz-, turning Latin platea into piazza.

piazzetta.etymology: Diminutive of piazza ('public square, plaza', < Classical Latin plătĕa, 'broad street, courtyard', borrowed from Ancient Greek πλατεῖα [ὁδός], plateîa [hodós], 'broad way') formed with -etta.

piccolo.etymology: Formed from the expressive childish/sound-symbolic root *pikk- ('small, tiny point', compare piccino, pizzico, Spanish pequeño) with the unstressed diminutive suffix -olo (< Latin -ŭlus).

piede.etymology: Continues Latin pēs, pĕdem ('foot'), with regular Tuscan diphthongisation of stressed open ĕ in an open syllable (pĕde > piede).
piede.notes: A piedi means 'on foot' (andare a piedi), and in piedi means 'standing up'.

piegare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin plĭcāre ('to fold, bend, roll up'), with regular Tuscan palatalization of initial pl- to pi- (/pj/), lowering of short ĭ to closed e, and voicing of intervocalic -c- to -g-.

pieghevole.etymology: Adjective derived from piegare ('to fold, bend', < Classical Latin plĭcāre) + the suffix -evole (< Latin -ĭbĭlis), meaning 'foldable, collapsible, pliable' (also substantivized for a folded 'brochure, leaflet').

pieno.etymology: Continues Classical Latin plēnus ('full, filled, complete'), from the Proto-Indo-European root *pleh₁- ('to fill'), with regular Tuscan palatalization of initial pl- to pi- (/pj/).

pietra.etymology: Continues Classical/Late Latin pĕtra ('rock, crag, stone'), borrowed from Ancient Greek πέτρα (pétra, 'rock, boulder'), which in Vulgar Latin displaced Classical lăpis, with regular Tuscan diphthongization of stressed short ĕ in an open syllable to ie.

pinzetta.etymology: Diminutive of pinza ('pincers, pliers, tongs', deverbal from pinzare, 'to pinch, nip, grip', of expressive origin *pints-* / reinforced by French pince and pincer) formed with -etta, designating 'tweezers, small tongs'.

history.meaning: to pinch, grip -> pliers, tongs -> tweezers, small tongs

pioggia.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *ploia for classical pluvia ('rain', from pluere, 'to rain'), with pl- > pi- and -vj- > -ddʒ-.
pioggia.notes: Notice how initial Latin pl- develops across Romance: Italian pioggia, French pluie, Spanish lluvia, Portuguese chuva.

piolo.etymology: Tuscan derivative (via *pediŏlum) of Latin pĕdĭcŭlus / pēs ('little foot, support peg, rung').

cognates.meaning: stake, post (from palus, parallel semantic field)

piolo.notes: Una scala a pioli ('stair with rungs') is how Italian distinguishes a portable ladder from a fixed staircase (una scala).

piovere.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *plŏvĕre (shifted to the third conjugation from Classical Latin plŭĕre / archaic plŏvĕre, 'to rain'), with regular Tuscan palatalization of initial pl- to pi- (/pj/).

piovigginare.etymology: Frequentative/attenuative verb formed within Italian from piovere ('to rain', < Vulgar Latin *plŏvĕre) with the suffix -igginare (compare caliginare), meaning 'to drizzle, rain lightly'.

pizzico.etymology: Deverbal noun from pizzicare ('to pinch, nip, tingle, pluck a string'), formed on the expressive/sound-symbolic root *pīts- / *pikk- ('sharp point, pinch, beak').

pizzo.etymology: Built on the expressive root *pīts- ('sharp point, peak, tip', whence 'pointed beard/goatee' and mountain 'peak'); the textile sense 'lace' arises from the pointed scallops or зубцы (merletti a pizzo) along the edge of lace trim.

più.etymology: Continues Classical Latin plūs ('more'), with regular Tuscan palatalization of initial pl- to pi- (/pj/) and loss of final -s (triggering syntactic gemination of a following consonant).

placca.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th–18th centuries from French plaque ('metal plate, badge, slab'), derived from Middle Dutch placke ('flat disk, coin, patch, metal plate').

history.meaning: plate, wall switch cover, badge, plaque

plastificato.etymology: Past-participial adjective of plastificare ('to coat or seal in plastic'), 20th-century compound of plastica ('plastic', < Latin plasticus < Ancient Greek plastikós, 'mouldable', from plássein, 'to mould') + verbalising -ficare (< Latin -ficāre, 'to make'). Its documented historical progression runs from Ancient Greek plastikós ('fit for moulding') -> 20th-century Italian plastificare -> plastificato ('to laminate -> laminated'). Cross-linguistic cognates include fr plastifié ('laminated, plastic-coated'), es plastificado ('laminated'); related Italian derivatives include plastica ('plastic'), plastificare ('to laminate'). Where English borrows Latin lamina ('thin plate') for 'laminated', Romance languages say plastificato / plastifié / plastificado.
plastificato.notes: Where English borrows Latin lamina ('thin plate') for 'laminated', Romance languages say plastificato / plastifié / plastificado.

poco.etymology: Continues Classical Latin paucus, paucum ('few, little'), with regular monophthongization of Latin au to open o.

history.meaning: little, a little, few, not much

poggiare.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *pŏdĭāre ('to ascend a hillock; to prop up, rest upon a pedestal or support', derived from Classical Latin pŏdĭum, 'elevated base, parapet, hillock', < Ancient Greek πόδιον, pódion), or apheretic form of appoggiare.

history.meaning: to rest upon a base, prop

poi.etymology: Continues Classical Latin pŏst ('after, behind, afterward') via Vulgar Latin *pŏs (before palatal/front sounds > poi).

polvere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin pŭlvis, pŭlvĕrem ('dust, powder, fine sand'), shifting in Italian from masculine to feminine gender, with regular lowering of short ŭ to closed o.

pomeriggio.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin pōmērīdĭum ('time after midday, afternoon', originally also the sacred strip of land behind the city wall), compound of post ('after') + mĕrīdĭēs ('midday, noon'), with regular Tuscan evolution of intervocalic -di- to -ggi- (/ddʒ/).

pomodoro.etymology: 16th-century compound of pomo d'oro ('golden apple'), naming the first yellow-fruited varieties brought from the Americas to Renaissance Italy.
pomodoro.notes: Pluralizes on the second element (i pomodori), though older literary Italian also recorded i pomidoro.

ponte.etymology: Continues Latin pontem (accusative of pōns, 'bridge'), keeping masculine gender in Italian (il ponte).

history.meaning: bridge; ship's deck; long holiday weekend

ponte.notes: Fare il ponte ('to make the bridge') means taking a working day off between a mid-week public holiday and the weekend.

porcellana.etymology: Originally the Old Italian name of the glossy cowrie shell (porcellana, from porcella, 'little sow'), extended by Marco Polo to translucent Chinese ceramic whose glaze resembled the shell.

history.meaning: glossy cowrie shell -> translucent Chinese ceramic

cognates.meaning: borrowed from Italian via Middle French

porcellana.notes: Marco Polo used Venetian/Italian porcellana ('cowrie shell') both for shell money in Asia and for gleaming Chinese ware, and Europe adopted the Italian word.

porta.etymology: Continues Latin porta ('city gate, doorway'), from the Indo-European root *per- ('to pass through'), cognate with porto ('harbour') and English port.

cognates.meaning: Latin loans and native Germanic cognate

rootFamily.gloss: heavy street doorway of a palazzo

porta.notes: Italian distinguishes una porta (room/house door), un portone (main street entrance of a building), and una portiera (car or carriage door).

portare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin pŏrtāre ('to carry, bear, convey, bring'), which in Vulgar Latin and Romance completely displaced ferre.

portone.etymology: Augmentative of porta ('door, gate', < Classical Latin pŏrta) formed with the suffix -one, designating the large main entrance door or carriage gate of an apartment building or palace.

history.meaning: large main entrance door, front building gate

posta.etymology: Substantivised feminine of posto / posita (< Late Latin posita, 'fixed relay station', feminine past participle of pōnĕre, 'to place, station'), originally naming the fixed stations along Italian roads where courier horses were stationed, and later the mail carried between them. Its documented historical progression runs from Classical Latin pōnĕre -> posita ('to place -> placed, stationed') -> Medieval / Renaissance Italian posta (cavalli di posta) ('fixed relay station for courier horses') -> Italian posta ('mail, postal service, post office'). Cross-linguistic cognates include fr poste ('mail, post office (borrowed from Italian!)'), es posta ('relay post'), en post / postal ('mail (borrowed via French from Italian posta!)'); related Italian derivatives include postale ('postal'), postino ('postman, mail carrier'), posto ('place, spot'). Renaissance Italian courier networks gave all of Europe—including English post and German Post—the word for mail!

history.meaning: fixed relay station for courier horses

cognates.meaning: mail (borrowed via French from Italian posta!)

posta.notes: Renaissance Italian courier networks gave all of Europe—including English post and German Post—the word for mail!

postale.etymology: Relational adjective formed from posta ('mail, courier relay', < Late Latin posita) + suffix -ale (< Latin -ālis). Its documented historical progression runs from Italian posta -> postale ('mail -> pertaining to the mail'). Cross-linguistic cognates include fr postal ('postal'), es postal ('postal; postcard'), en postal ('relating to mail'); related Italian derivatives include posta ('mail, post'), postino ('postman'), cartolina postale ('postcard'). Appears in key everyday compounds: ufficio postale ('post office'), timbro postale ('postmark'), cassetta postale ('letterbox').
postale.notes: Appears in key everyday compounds: ufficio postale ('post office'), timbro postale ('postmark'), cassetta postale ('letterbox').

postino.etymology: Derived within Italian from posta ('mail, postal service', from Medieval Latin pŏsĭta [stătĭō], 'fixed relay station where couriers changed horses', feminine past participle of pōnĕre) + the occupational suffix -ino.

posto.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin pŏstus, syncopated from Classical Latin pŏsĭtus ('placed, set, situated', past participle of pōnĕre, 'to put, place'), substantivized in the masculine (il posto) for 'place, spot, seat, job position'.

history.meaning: place, spot, seat, space, job; placed (participle)

potere.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *potēre, regularized from classical posse ('to be able', contraction of potis esse).

history.meaning: can, to be able to; power (il potere)

cognates.meaning: via Anglo-Norman poeir and Latin potēns

potere.notes: In compound tenses, modal potere takes the auxiliary (essere or avere) required by the following infinitive: non sono potuto venire vs. non ho potuto mangiare.

povero.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *paupĕrus (remodeled as a first/second-declension adjective from Classical Latin third-declension paupĕr, paupĕrem, 'producing little, poor, scanty', from paucus + parĕre), with monophthongization of au to open o.

pranzo.etymology: Continues Classical Latin prandĭum ('late-morning or midday meal, luncheon', from *prām-ed-iom, 'first eating'), reshaped in Tuscan via prandio / desinare or back-formed from pranzare (< *prandiāre), with evolution of -di- after -n- to the dental affricate -z-.

preciso.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin praecīsus ('cut off in front, shortened, brief, clear-cut, exact'), past participle of praecīdĕre ('to cut off in front, abridge', from prae- + caedĕre, 'to cut').

history.meaning: to cut off cleanly -> clear-cut, exact, precise

preferire.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin praeferre ('to carry in front, hold before, prefer', compound of prae- 'before' + ferre 'to bear, carry'), adapted to the fourth conjugation (-ire).

preferito.etymology: Participial adjective and noun from preferire ('to prefer', < Classical Latin praeferre), meaning 'favorite, preferred'.

pregare.etymology: Continues Classical Latin prĕcārī (Vulgar Latin active *prĕcāre, 'to ask earnestly, beg, entreat, pray', derived from prĕx, prĕcis, 'prayer, entreaty'), with regular voicing of intervocalic -c- to -g-.

history.meaning: to pray, beg, ask politely (ti prego)

prego.etymology: First-person singular of pregare ('to pray, ask earnestly'), from Latin precārī; shortened from vi/La prego ('I beg you / please do') into Italian's all-purpose courteous reply.

history.meaning: 'I pray you' -> you're welcome; please go ahead; pardon?

cognates.meaning: parallel polite reply from prier (< precārī)
exact functional parallel ('I ask' -> please / you're welcome)

prego.notes: Italian's Swiss-army-knife courtesy word: answers grazie ('you're welcome'), invites someone through a door or to sit ('after you / please'), or asks 'how may I help you?' in shops.

premere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin prĕmĕre ('to press, squeeze, push down, bear upon').

prendere.etymology: Continues Classical Latin prĕhĕndĕre / prēndĕre ('to lay hold of, grasp, seize, take', compound of prae- + *hendĕre, cognate with English get).

prenotare.etymology: Learned or administrative compound formed from Classical Latin praenŏtāre ('to mark beforehand, note down in advance', from prae- 'before' + nŏtāre 'to mark, record'), specialized in modern Italian for 'to book, reserve in advance'.

prenotazione.etymology: Action noun derived within Italian from prenotare ('to book, reserve in advance', < Latin praenŏtāre) + the suffix -zione (< Latin -tiō, -tiōnem).

preoccuparsi.etymology: Reflexive form of preoccupare, learned continuation of Classical Latin praeoccŭpāre ('to seize beforehand, occupy the mind in advance', from prae- + occŭpāre); in reflexive use, 'to worry, be anxious, take care of'.

history.meaning: to seize beforehand, engross the mind
to trouble -> to worry, be concerned

preparare.etymology: Learned or semi-learned continuation of Classical Latin praepărāre ('to make ready beforehand, prepare, equip'), compound of prae- ('beforehand') + părāre ('to make ready, furnish').

preparazione.etymology: Learned borrowing from Classical Latin praeparātiō, -ōnis ('a making ready beforehand'), action noun from praeparāre (from prae-, 'before', + parāre, 'to make ready, set in order').
preparazione.notes: In Italian, avere una grande preparazione also means having thorough training and mastery in one's craft.

pressione.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin prĕssĭō, prĕssĭōnem ('act of pressingdown, pressure, leverage'), derived from prĕmĕre ('to press', past participle prĕssus).

presto.etymology: Continues Late Latin praestus ('ready, at hand, prompt, quick'), adjectival back-formation from the Classical Latin adverb praestō ('at hand, ready, present', in praestō esse), used in Italian both as an adverb ('soon, early, quickly') and as an adjective ('quick, ready').

previsione.etymology: Learned formation from Late Latin praevīsĭō, praevīsĭōnem ('foreseeing, foresight'), derived from Classical Latin praevĭdēre ('to see beforehand, foresee', past participle praevīsus).

previsto.etymology: Past participle of prevedere ('to foresee, expect, provide for', < Classical Latin praevĭdēre, from prae- + vĭdēre), formed on the model of visto (past participle of vedere).

history.meaning: to foresee, expect -> foreseen, expected, scheduled

prezioso.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin prĕtĭōsus ('of great value, costly, precious'), derived from prĕtĭum ('price, worth, value').

prezzemolo.etymology: Inherited via Vulgar Latin *petrosīmolum from Classical Latin petroselīnum ('parsley'), borrowed from Ancient Greek πετροσέλινον (petrosélinon, 'rock celery', compound of πέτρα, pétra, 'rock, stone', + σέλινον, sélinon, 'celery'). The wild plant grows naturally in rocky Mediterranean crevices.

cognates.meaning: aromatic herb (from the same Greek compound via Old French peresil)

prezzemolo.notes: Astonishingly, English parsley, French persil, Spanish perejil, and Italian prezzemolo all descend from the same four-word Greek compound petrosélinon ('rock-celery')!

prezzo.etymology: Continues Classical Latin prĕtĭum ('worth, value, price, reward'), with regular Tuscan evolution of postvocalic -ti- to geminate dental affricate -zz- (/tts/).

prima.etymology: Continues Classical Latin prīma (feminine singular or neuter plural of prīmus, 'first', originally in temporal phrases such as prīmā hōrā, 'at the first hour'), functioning as an adverb ('before, earlier, first') and noun ('first class/gear, premiere').

primavera.etymology: Continues Vulgar Latin *prīma vēra, from Classical Latin prīmō vēre ('at the start of spring', from prīmus 'first' and vēr 'spring').
primavera.notes: Classical Latin distinguished *prīma vēra ('early spring, floral awakening') from *prīmum tempus (> French printemps); in Italian cuisine alla primavera means served with fresh spring vegetables.

primo.etymology: Continues Classical Latin prīmus ('first, foremost', superlative built on the prepositional root *pro- / prae-, 'before, in front').

principale.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin prīncĭpālis ('first, original, chief, principal'), derived from prīnceps, prīncĭpis ('first in order, chief, leader', from prīmus + capĕre).

privato.etymology: Learned continuation of Classical Latin prīvātus ('apart from the state, belonging to an individual, personal, private', originally past participle of prīvāre, 'to set apart, deprive', from prīvus, 'single, one's own').

history.meaning: single, one's own -> to separate -> private, personal

problema.etymology: Learned borrowing from Classical Latin prŏblēma ('question proposed for academic discussion, riddle'), from Ancient Greek πρόβλημα (próblēma, 'something thrown forward, jutting obstacle, task or question put forward', from προβάλλειν, probállein).
